title: Practical Mandarin
levelBasis: Independent communicative teaching progression. Reference bands are provenance only, not competence or examination claims.
reviewPolicy: Modules span several lessons of about 5-8 new senses. Select relevant earlier and fragile items for retrieval, revisit them on later days, and record the modality and assistance. Inventory coverage is not demonstrated mastery.

levels.title: First contact
goals: Introduce yourself and repair a misunderstanding.
Ask about a small quantity or price.

checkpoint.task: Complete a short introduction and purchase with an unfamiliar partner and a changed quantity.
criteria: Introduce yourself and repair a misunderstanding.
Ask about a small quantity or price.

modules.title: First exchanges and communication repair
modules.outcome: Greet someone politely, introduce yourself by name and as a student, return a question, and say that you do not understand.

modules.title: Drinks and polite requests
modules.outcome: Ask politely for coffee, tea, water, or milk, offer someone a drink or a seat, and accept or decline an offer.

modules.title: Numbers, quantities, and prices
modules.outcome: Order a specified number of drinks or objects, ask how many or how much, and understand prices up to one hundred yuan.

levels.title: People, belongings, and places
goals: Identify objects by color and size.
Ask where a person or place is.

checkpoint.task: Identify a missing object and explain whose it is and where it might be.
criteria: Identify objects by color and size.
Ask where a person or place is.

modules.title: Colors and describing objects
modules.outcome: Identify a cup, bag, or book by pointing, name six basic colors, describe an object's size, and ask what something is.

modules.title: Family, friends, and belongings
modules.outcome: Introduce family members and friends, say what you have or do not have, and identify whose book, bag, or phone it is.

modules.title: People and everyday places
modules.outcome: Identify teachers and doctors, ask where everyday places are, and say who or what is at a location.

levels.title: Daily activities
goals: Choose food and clarify a purchase.

checkpoint.task: Arrange an activity and a meal using a new combination of times and preferences.
criteria: Choose food and clarify a purchase.

modules.title: Time and daily routines
modules.outcome: Ask and answer when someone gets up, eats, works, or sleeps, and say where an everyday activity happens.

modules.title: Interests and learned abilities
modules.outcome: Say what you like doing, describe what you can read, write, or perform, and identify an interest you share with someone.

modules.title: Food and everyday shopping
modules.outcome: Buy familiar foods including apples, ask about prices, describe what tastes good, and say what everyone in a group wants to eat.

levels.title: Getting help and making plans
goals: Ask for directions and explain a destination.
Agree on a simple meeting plan.

checkpoint.task: Resolve a short travel or scheduling problem without an item-specific answer model.
criteria: Ask for directions and explain a destination.
Agree on a simple meeting plan.

modules.title: Directions and getting around
modules.outcome: Ask where a destination is, identify its position relative to a landmark, and say where you are going and what you intend to do there.

modules.title: Asking for help and permission
modules.outcome: Ask for help finding an item, request repetition, ask permission to use something, and tell someone not to take an item or open a door.

modules.title: Making plans and independent exchanges
modules.outcome: Exchange phone numbers, agree on a date and time to meet, check availability with an A-not-A question, and complete a short plan without switching languages.

grammar.english: S is a person or thing
grammar.note: Identity uses a noun predicate; do not insert this verb before ordinary adjectives.

grammar.english: S does not; S is not
grammar.note: Use for habitual or intended actions and most adjective negation; not possession.

grammar.english: What about this person or thing?
grammar.note: A short return question relies on the preceding conversational topic.

examples.english: I am well. What about you?
My book is here. What about yours?

grammar.note: Append to a statement for a neutral yes-no question; retain statement word order.

grammar.english: S would like to do something
grammar.note: Express desire or intention; a following verb is not inflected.

examples.english: I would like to drink some water.
Where would you like to go?

grammar.note: A polite request still needs an appropriate tone and context.
Select a classifier with the noun; learn noun-classifier pairs rather than a universal substitute.

examples.english: Please give me a glass of water.

grammar.note: The first commonly expects a small count; the second allows an open quantity.

examples.english: How many books do you have?

grammar.english: S is adjective; often neutral rather than very
grammar.note: A plain adjective predicate commonly takes a degree adverb; stress changes intensity.
Demonstratives before a counted noun normally take a classifier.

examples.english: That person is my older brother.

grammar.pattern: 谁 / 什么 / 哪儿 in the answer slot
grammar.note: Question words stay where the answer would occur; do not add a yes-no particle.
Use for possession; the object need not be definite.
Possession takes this negative rather than ordinary predicate negation.

examples.english: I do not have a car.

grammar.note: This links an owner or modifier to a noun; it may be omitted in close family relationships.
A location predicate differs from an identity predicate.

examples.english: My book is on the table.

grammar.english: There is something at a place
grammar.note: Introduce an indefinite entity using a place-first existential construction.

examples.english: There is a book on the table.
There are many students in the school.

grammar.note: Coordinate noun phrases; do not use this automatically to connect full clauses.

examples.english: My older sister and I go to school.
There is tea and water on the table.

grammar.pattern: time + S + verb / S + time + verb
grammar.note: Place time before the verb, often before or after the subject; no tense conjugation.

examples.english: Tomorrow I am going to school.
I am studying at home today.

grammar.english: S does something at a place
grammar.note: Put the location phrase before the main action.

grammar.english: S also does or is something
grammar.note: Place this adverb before the verb or adjective, not after an object.

grammar.english: S knows how to do something
grammar.note: This use marks a learned skill, not permission or every kind of physical ability.

grammar.english: all members do or are something
grammar.note: The scope normally refers back to people or things already introduced.

grammar.english: go / come somewhere to do something
grammar.note: A serial-verb sequence expresses movement followed by purpose.

examples.english: I am going to the shop to buy water.
He is coming to my home to eat.

grammar.note: Use for a direct prohibition or preventive request; soften with context when needed.

grammar.english: whether someone does or is something
grammar.note: A-not-A creates a yes-no question with a verb or adjective; avoid adding another yes-no question particle.
